title: Docs: compare `server + index.tsx` vs traditional Shiny app development
description:
# Docs: compare `server + index.tsx` vs traditional Shiny app development

## Summary

Shiny already supports both app shapes:

- **Traditional** — `app.py` defines the UI in Python (`ui.page_fluid(...)`) and the server function; the framework ships rendered HTML (and paired JS) over the websocket and patches it into the page.
- **`server + index.html`** — a static `www/index.html` is the entry point and the Python file is server-only. Core Shiny supports this today.

`shinyreact` adopts the second shape but changes *what crosses the websocket*. Instead of the server sending fully-formed DOM fragments plus matching JavaScript, it sends **only JSON data**. The UI business logic — which component to render, how to lay it out, how interaction maps to state — lives in the client (`index.tsx` / `app.js`). This is the actual difference worth documenting; the file layout is secondary.

External users landing on this repo today have no single page that explains this distinction or helps them decide which pattern fits their app.

## Audience

External Shiny users (Python) evaluating `shinyreact` — including people who have never written React and are weighing whether moving UI logic to the client is worth the learning curve.

## Proposed location

A new top-level doc, e.g. `docs/spa-vs-traditional.md`, linked from the README and from `docs/features.md`.

## What the page should cover

1. **Framing — what's actually different**
   - Both patterns are valid Shiny apps.
   - The difference is *where UI logic lives* and *what travels over the websocket*:
     - Traditional: server owns UI logic; HTML fragments + JS travel the wire.
     - `shinyreact` (`server + index.tsx`): client owns UI logic; only JSON data travels the wire.
   - Note that `server + index.html` already exists in core Shiny — `shinyreact` is specifically about pushing UI construction to the client on top of that shape.

2. **Side-by-side file layout**
   - Traditional: single `app.py` with `app_ui = ui.page_fluid(...)` + server function.
   - `shinyreact`: `app.py` (server logic only) + `www/index.html` + `www/index.tsx` (or plain `app.js` for no-build apps).
   - Point at concrete examples: `11-columns-traditional` vs `12-columns-spa`, `1-hello-world` vs `13-spa-hello`.

3. **What goes over the websocket**
   - Traditional: input values up; HTML/JS render output down (`render.ui`, output bindings producing markup).
   - `shinyreact`: input values up via `useShinyInput`; pure JSON data down via `@reactive_output`. The client decides how to turn that data into DOM.
   - Implications: smaller, structured payloads; no server-driven DOM patching; client can re-render without a round-trip.

4. **Dev workflow**
   - Traditional: edit `app.py`, reload. No JS toolchain.
   - `shinyreact`: two flavors — (a) hand-written `React.createElement` in `app.js`, no build step; (b) JSX + Vite, `shiny run` handles the build.

5. **Tradeoffs** (strengths/weaknesses, not "winner")
   - Traditional strengths: zero JS required, terse for forms/reports, server-side rendering on first paint, mature ecosystem.
   - Traditional weaknesses: dynamic UI requires observer-lifecycle bookkeeping; every interaction is a server round-trip; UI and data are tightly coupled in `render.ui`.
   - `shinyreact` strengths: client owns UI state (no observer churn for drag/sort/filter), lower-latency interactions, modern React patterns, easier to style with shadcn/Tailwind, the wire format is inspectable JSON.
   - `shinyreact` weaknesses: requires reading/writing React (or trusting an AI to), introduces a client/server split to reason about, more moving parts for trivial apps.

6. **"Pick this if…" guidance**
   - Traditional: forms, reports, dashboards with mostly static layout, teams with no JS experience.
   - `shinyreact`: rich interactivity (drag-and-drop, live filtering, custom components), shadcn/Tailwind styling, apps where client responsiveness matters or where keeping the wire format as data (not HTML) is valuable.

7. **Migration note** — patterns coexist; `shinyreact` continues to work, and a `SpaApp` can be one piece of a larger system.

## Out of scope

- API reference for `SpaApp` / `reactive_output` (lives elsewhere).
- The R package (not yet implemented).
- Performance benchmarks — qualitative tradeoffs only for v1.

## Acceptance

> **Note:** This work delivers `docs/spa-vs-traditional.md` directly as part of the `shinyreact` rename/unification in `docs/superpowers/plans/2026-05-05-shinyreact-merge.md`.

- [ ] `docs/spa-vs-traditional.md` exists and covers the seven sections above.
- [ ] Page makes clear that `server + index.html` is core Shiny, and the novel piece is moving UI logic to the client (JSON-only over the wire).
- [ ] Linked from README and from `docs/features.md`.
- [ ] Each pattern points at a runnable example in `pkg-py/examples/`.

title: Rename `render_json` to `reactive_output` to mirror `useShinyOutput`
description:
## Background: the naming rationale

In the SPA-first `shinyreact` package, `@reactive_output` is the server-side counterpart to the client-side `useShinyOutput()` hook.

The old name read like a UI renderer — something that produces HTML or a DOM node — but it does neither. There is no UI binding, no output placeholder, no rendering. It is plumbing: a reactive value that gets serialized to JSON and shipped over the websocket to a `useShinyOutput("id")` hook on the client.

The asymmetry was clear when putting the four pieces side by side:

| Direction | Server | Client hook |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Client → Server | `input.x()` | `useShinyInput("x", ...)` |
| Server → Client | `@reactive_output` ✓ | `useShinyOutput("x", ...)` |

The input side reads naturally — `input` on the server pairs with `useShinyInput` on the client. The output side did not. A developer learning the SPA model had to be told what the old decorator name meant — it did not communicate the `useShinyOutput` pairing by itself.

## Proposal: `reactive_output` — the unified decorator

> **Updated:** `reactive_output` is now the **unified** decorator for both SPA and traditional patterns. It accepts `Spec | Node | Jsonifiable`, drops `extra_deps` (use `ui_output(id, extra_deps=[...])` instead), and is delivered by the `shinyreact` merge work in `docs/superpowers/plans/2026-05-05-shinyreact-merge.md`.

```python
import shinyreact

@shinyreact.reactive_output
def scatter_data():
    return {\"age\": [1, 2, 3], \"score\": [10, 20, 30]}
```

```tsx
const data = useShinyOutput(\"scatter_data\", null);
```

The name now states what the decorator does: it declares a reactive value that is exposed as an output over the websocket. The pairing with `useShinyOutput` is obvious from the name alone, and the symmetry with `input` / `useShinyInput` is restored:

| Direction | Server | Client hook |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Client → Server | `input.x()` | `useShinyInput(\"x\", ...)` |
| Server → Client | `@reactive_output` | `useShinyOutput(\"x\", ...)` |

## Why \"reactive_output\" specifically

- **`reactive_`** signals that this is a reactive primitive on par with `@reactive.calc` / `@reactive.effect`, not a UI renderer in the traditional Shiny `@render.*` family. In the SPA model there are no `@render.plot` / `@render.text` decorators — the server emits values, not UI.
- **`_output`** mirrors the client hook (`useShinyOutput`) and the existing Shiny vocabulary for the server→client direction.
- It avoids `render_*`, which in Shiny historically means \"produce UI for an output binding\". This decorator does not do that.

## Considered alternatives

- **`reactive.output`** (as a member of the `reactive` namespace, like `reactive.calc`) — arguably even cleaner, but would require coordinating with core Shiny's `reactive` module. A top-level `shinyreact.reactive_output` is a smaller, self-contained change.
- **`output_json`** — keeps the JSON suffix but still reads like a UI thing and does not match `useShinyOutput`.
- **`ws_output` / `socket_output`** — accurate but exposes transport details the user shouldn't have to care about.
- **Leave as `reactive_output`** — cheapest, but the name actively misleads new users about what the SPA model is.

## Scope

- Rename file and function in `pkg-py/src/shinyreact/` and `__init__.py` to `reactive_output`.
- Update tests in `pkg-py/tests/`.
- Update SPA examples (13–16) and `docs/features.md`.
- This covers the unified `shinyreact` package (both SPA and traditional patterns).
- Pre-1.0, so no deprecation shim needed — but happy to add one if reviewers prefer.

## Out of scope

- The typed-contract / `InputModel` / `OutputModel` work in #50 and #30. This rename is orthogonal and complementary: if those land, `reactive_output` is still the right name for the imperative decorator form.

title: Rename shinyjson → shinyreact
description:
## Summary

> **Plan and spec:** `docs/superpowers/specs/2026-05-05-shinyreact-merge-design.md`, `docs/superpowers/plans/2026-05-05-shinyreact-merge.md`.
> **Status:** The rename has happened. The traditional JSON-spec pattern is **kept** (not retired) — both patterns are now available under the unified `shinyreact` package.

The package has been renamed to `shinyreact`. The traditional JSON-spec pattern has been unified back into `shinyreact` alongside the SPA-first API. Users now have one package covering both development patterns.

## Why rename

The package's job is wiring Python reactive compute into a React SPA. The JSON on the wire is implementation detail, not the product. Today's name answers a question users don't ask (\"how do I work with JSON in Shiny?\") instead of the one they do (\"how do I use Shiny with React?\").

Concrete benefits:

- **Symmetry with the npm side.** `@posit/shiny-react` (npm) ↔ `shinyreact` (PyPI). Same name across both ecosystems for new users to learn once.
- **Future-proof for non-React bindings.** Leaves room for `shinyvue`, `shinysvelte`, `shinysolid` as parallel packages later (see #32) without forcing the name `shinyreact` to mean \"the React variant\" by convention.
- **Discoverability.** `pip search shinyreact`, GitHub search \"shiny react\", Stack Overflow tags — they all land on the right package immediately.
- **Architectural clarity.** The SPA-first pivot is a hard course correction (`DESIGN.md` §1). The name `shinyreact` points at what matters — React + Shiny — rather than the JSON wire format.

## Why bundle with the unification

A separate rename release would mean two migrations in two releases:

1. \"`shinyreact` is gone, switch to `shinyreact`.\"
2. \"`shinyreact` is now `shinyreact`.\"

Bundling makes it one migration:

> The package family is now just `shinyreact`. If you were migrating from the old separate packages, one migration covers everything.

One release, one set of release notes, one upgrade for users.

## Scope of the rename

### Code (all completed ✓)

- Python package path renamed: `pkg-py/src/shinyreact/`
- `pkg-py/tests/` imports updated
- `pyproject.toml`: `name = \"shinyreact\"`, hatchling package path updated
- JS/CSS files renamed to `shinyreact.js`, `shinyreact.css`
- Global renamed to `window.shinyreact` (with a transitional alias kept for one release; see below)
- `HTMLDependency(name=\"shinyreact\", ...)`
- CSS class renamed to `\"shinyreact-output\"`
- All examples updated
- `Makefile` targets updated
- `CLAUDE.md`, `DESIGN.md`, `docs/STATUS.md`, `docs/timeline.md`, `decisions/*` updated

### Function names — kept as-is

`reactive_output` stays `reactive_output`. It accurately describes what it does (ships JSON to `useShinyOutput`), and renaming it would force every existing app to update both its import *and* its decorators. Package name and function name are separable decisions.

`SpaApp` stays `SpaApp`.

### Repo/org

- Repo is now `posit-dev/shinyreact` (GitHub auto-redirects old links).
- All open issues at filing time (#27 through #37 plus this one) carry forward unchanged.

### PyPI

- Publish first `shinyreact` release.
- Yank or deprecate `shinyreact` on PyPI: ship a final \"renamed to shinyreact, install that instead\" version; do not silently re-export.

### npm

- The bundled IIFE filename is `shinyreact.js` ✓ done. The (separate) `@posit/shiny-react` npm package per #28 is unaffected by this rename.

## Migration guide content

A migration doc covers:

- Update imports: use `import shinyreact`
- Update function imports: `from shinyreact import SpaApp, reactive_output`
- Update JS global calls: `window.shinyreact.registerComponents(...)`
- Update any hand-written HTML: use `class=\"shinyreact-output\"`
- HTMLDependency name change: `name=\"shinyreact\"` (rare — only affects users hand-rolling deps)

## Transitional alias — one release only

For the renamed-release only, these deprecated aliases were kept (emitting `DeprecationWarning`) ✓ done:

- `import shinyreact` (old name) → re-exports `shinyreact` symbols.
- Old global → still defined; same object as `window.shinyreact`.
- Old CSS class still recognized by the binding alongside `\"shinyreact-output\"`. ✓ done

Removed in the next release after the rename. The point of the alias is only to give downstream packages and the example gallery one release cycle to follow.

## Open questions

- **Do we publish `shinyreact` to PyPI before the rename release, as a stake?** Squatting the name reduces the risk that someone else takes it. Probably yes — register an empty 0.0.1 once #37 is merged but before the rename ships.
- **Org/repo rename timing.** GitHub redirects make this safe to do at any time, but bundling with the rename release minimizes surprise. Lean: rename repo at release time.
- **Does anything in `posit-dev/shiny-react` (npm) move into this repo?** Out of scope here — kept under #28's umbrella.
- **Documentation site / domain.** If/when there's a docs site, the URL should track the rename too. Not relevant today; flag for later.
- **Does the rename change the CSS class prefix in user CSS?** Yes (`shinyreact-output` → `shinyreact-output`). Documented in the migration guide. Transitional alias for one release.

## Relationship to other issues

- **#37 (Retire old packages):** The retirement track was reversed — the traditional JSON-spec pattern is folded back into `shinyreact` alongside the SPA-first API. The rename and unification have happened in the same release.
- **Touches #28** (`@posit/shiny` as npm package) cosmetically — no architectural overlap, but the migration doc should mention both for users tracking the broader ecosystem.
- **Touches #32** (UI-framework npm bindings) — once renamed, the per-framework binding template uses `shinyreact` as the Python peer name in its docs.
- **Touches #34** (scaffolding skill) — the skill's templates need updating in lockstep with the rename.

## Out of scope

- Renaming `reactive_output`, `SpaApp`, `Spec`, `Element`, `Node`, or any other API symbol.
- Rebranding (logo, marketing, posit::conf talk titles) — separate concern.
- R package naming — irrelevant until the R package exists.

title: Retire shinyjsonold once SPA-first parity is proven
description:
## Summary

Track the eventual removal of the legacy JSON-spec package (`shinyjsonold`) once the new SPA-first `shinyjson` package has demonstrably absorbed its use cases. Not actionable now — this issue exists to make the decision concrete and prevent drift.

The split (commit `562b5a2`) is recent. `DESIGN.md` §8 frames SPA-first as *a prototype to evaluate*, not a decided architecture. Removing the alternative before the evaluation finishes would collapse the option space too early. But shipping two parallel packages indefinitely is also wrong: it bloats the test matrix, splits documentation, and makes it harder to commit to a single user-facing story.

## Exit criteria — when to remove

`shinyjsonold` gets removed in the next release after **all** of these are true:

1. **Example parity.** Each of examples 1–9 (currently `shinyjsonold`) has a SPA-first equivalent that:
   - Matches or beats the original on lines of server code.
   - Matches or beats the original on perceived complexity (no new build-step pain that the original didn't have, or a clear story for why the build step is worth it).
   - Demos at the same visual quality.
2. **No regressions in the showcase set.** The four pillar demos — `1-hello-world`, `3-outputs`, `5-shadcn`, `6-dashboard` — work cleanly under SPA-first with no \"but you can't do X anymore\" caveats.
3. **At least one dynamic-UI case settled.** The JSON-spec model's clearest strength is server-driven UI shape (not just data). Before retiring it, we need at least one real example of a SPA-first equivalent for a dynamic-UI pattern (e.g. \"server adds a new card to the dashboard at runtime\"). If we can't, that's a signal to keep `shinyjsonold` longer or to design a SPA-first dynamic-UI primitive first.
4. **No active external dependencies.** No internal demos, design partners, or downstream packages still pinned to `shinyjsonold`. (Verified by a quick survey of known consumers.)
5. **`docs/STATUS.md` TODOs scoped.** Several legacy-only TODOs exist (\"What is the general shape of a UI component?\", \"Can dynamic UI be supported?\", parts of \"What render methods are useful?\"). They should either be answered (because SPA-first answered them differently) or closed as obsolete — not left dangling.

## Removal mechanics — when criteria are met

- Delete `pkg-py/src/shinyjsonold/` and `pkg-py/tests/old/`.
- Drop `@json-render/react` from `js/package.json`. Verify bundle shrinks.
- Either delete examples 1–9 or replace them in-place with their SPA-first equivalents (probably the latter — preserves URLs and example numbering).
- Drop the `## Parallel packages` heading and \"shinyjsonold\" mentions from `docs/STATUS.md` and `CLAUDE.md`.
- Drop \"shinyjsonold\" mentions from `DESIGN.md` (§8 and the appendix). The \"Previous Explorations\" appendix can stay as historical context but should be edited to past tense.
- One-time deprecation release: ship a final `shinyjsonold` version with a deprecation notice, then remove. Or remove cleanly if no external users exist (per criterion 4).

## Why a trigger and not a date

A calendar deadline (\"by 2026-06-01\") would force the decision regardless of whether the SPA-first prototype has actually proven itself. Criteria-based removal is honest about what we're learning: the prototype either earns the slot or it doesn't.

If criteria 1–3 are still unmet at posit::conf, that itself is signal — the SPA-first thesis needs more work before retiring the alternative.

## Status snapshot (date filed)

- Examples 1–9 still on `shinyjsonold`.
- Examples 10–12 are rough SPA-first prototypes (per `docs/STATUS.md`'s \"Clean up example apps\" TODO).
- Examples 13–16 are clean SPA-first demos (hello, columns, columns+shadcn, full shadcn).

So we have ~4 SPA-first examples and 9 legacy ones. Criterion 1 (parity) is roughly half-met by the columns demos (ex 11 traditional ↔ ex 14/15 SPA-first); the other showcase pieces need ports.

## Out of scope

- The R package, which is still a placeholder regardless.
- Whether to keep the `@json-render/react` dependency for some other purpose.
- Decisions about specific replacement examples — handled in the example-cleanup TODO.

title: Ship shiny-react bindings as npm packages for popular UI frameworks
description:
## Summary

Each example that uses a real component library (shadcn in ex 15/16) re-implements the same plumbing: Vite lib-mode IIFE, externalize React to `window.shinyreact`, register components, wire `useShinyInput`/`useShinyOutput` into a handful of components. That's ~50 lines of boilerplate per app, plus a `vite.config.js` people copy-paste.

We should publish a family of small npm packages — one per UI framework — that ship the bindings pre-wired. Users `npm install @shinyreact/shadcn` (or `@shinyreact/mui`, etc.) and get framework components that already speak Shiny.

## Why

- Removes the per-app Vite config boilerplate.
- Gives each framework a single, versioned source of truth for the React-side contract.
- Makes the \"how do I use library X with Shiny?\" answer a one-line install instead of an example to copy.
- Bigger ecosystems (Material, Ant, Mantine) bring their own users who'd otherwise never touch shinyreact.

## Candidate packages

Tier 1 (highest demand, likely owned by us):
- `@shinyreact/shadcn` — wraps shadcn/ui primitives + lucide icons. Ex 15/16 collapse to ~5 lines.
- `@shinyreact/mui` — Material UI v6.
- `@shinyreact/bootstrap` — React Bootstrap (or react-bootstrap-icons).

Tier 2 (community-driven, we provide a template):
- `@shinyreact/mantine`
- `@shinyreact/antd`
- `@shinyreact/chakra`
- `@shinyreact/headlessui` + Tailwind
- `@shinyreact/radix` (lower-level than shadcn)

Tier 3 (data-viz oriented, overlaps with #31):
- `@shinyreact/plotly`
- `@shinyreact/echarts`
- `@shinyreact/ag-grid`

## What each package contains

- React components (or thin wrappers) that accept the underlying library's props **plus** an optional `shinyId`. With `shinyId`, the component round-trips state through `useShinyInput` and exposes commands via `useShinyMessageHandler`.
- A pre-built IIFE bundle with React/ReactDOM externalized to `window.shinyreact` (matching ex 15's `vite.config.js`).
- A registration entry point: importing the package side-effectfully calls `window.shinyreact.registerComponents(...)` so JSON specs reference the components by name.
- Optional Python companion: a sibling Python package (`shinyshadcn`, `shinymui`, …) with `extra_deps = [...]` and any `Spec`/`Element` builders. Already established pattern — see `CLAUDE.md` §\"Downstream package pattern\".
- TypeScript types for every component, including the round-trip input shapes (so #30's typegen has something to read).

## Repo / publishing strategy

- One monorepo per package family — likely `posit-dev/shinyreact-bindings` with each package at `packages/shadcn`, `packages/mui`, etc.
- Or each non-trivial one gets its own repo (lighter ownership coupling).
- Versioning policy: each binding pins a peer dependency on `@shinyreact/core` (the bundle we ship from `js/`). Major bumps in shinyreact core require a major bump in each binding.
- A `create-shinyreact-app` scaffolder picks a binding and generates the matching `app.py` + `vite.config.js` + `src/main.jsx`.

## Open questions

- **Do these need to be published as npm packages at all?** For SPA-first apps the user already has a Vite build — they could install directly. But \"copy this config\" is friction; an npm package is the natural unit.
- **Granularity**: one package per framework (`@shinyreact/shadcn`) or one package per component family (`@shinyreact/shadcn-card`, `@shinyreact/shadcn-form`)? Probably per-framework; tree-shaking handles unused components.
- **Python sibling packaging**: do we ship the Python companion in the same repo as the JS binding (mirroring this repo's `js/` + `pkg-py/` layout) or split? Same repo is simpler; split is cleaner if a JS-only or Python-only audience shows up.
- **shadcn specifically is copy-paste-source, not an npm package.** Our `@shinyreact/shadcn` would either (a) re-publish the shadcn primitives, which fights the upstream model, or (b) ship a CLI that runs `npx shadcn add` and patches in the Shiny wiring. (b) is more honest.
- **Theming**: `_brand.yml` story for each framework. Bootstrap and shadcn already have brand.yml integration; MUI/Mantine/Antd would need adapters.
- **Maintenance burden**: 6+ frameworks each tracking their own breaking changes is a lot of surface. We probably ship 2 (shadcn, MUI) and document a binding-author template for the rest.
- **Governance**: which bindings does Posit own vs. community? Likely Posit owns shadcn + bootstrap (existing R parity); community owns the rest with a template repo.

## Relationship to other work

- Depends on #28 (Shiny client runtime as an npm package) — without that, every binding has to re-vendor or peer-depend on the IIFE bundle.
- Pairs with #30 — typed inputs/outputs in Python comes \"for free\" if each binding ships TS types for its round-trip inputs.
- Pairs with #31 — enhanced renderers are the natural Python counterpart; `@shinyreact/plotly` ships React side, `shinyplotly` Python ships matching `render_plotly`.

## Out of scope

- R package equivalents for each binding.
- Vue / Svelte / Solid bindings — react-only for now.

title: Enhanced renderers: expose round-trip inputs and update methods on the renderer
description:
## Summary

Today a `@reactive_output` (or any future `@render_plotly`, `@render_table_react`, etc.) is a one-way pipe: Python returns a value, the React component renders it. But many useful components also send signals *back* — selected rows, brushed regions, zoom extents, expanded nodes — and accept *commands* — \"reset zoom\", \"select row 4\", \"update plot limits\".

Today users would wire those by hand: pick `useShinyInput` names in JSX, declare matching `inputs.<name>` in Python, send `custom_message`s via `session.send_custom_message` for the command direction. Each downstream package re-invents the contract.

We should let the renderer *be* that contract. Inputs the component emits become fields on the renderer; commands the component accepts become methods on the renderer. The renderer already owns the output ID and has the session in scope, so it has everything it needs.

## Precedent

`@render.data_frame` in Shiny for Python already does this:

```python
@render.data_frame
def grid():
    return render.DataGrid(df, selection_mode=\"rows\")

@reactive.effect
def _():
    rows = grid.cell_selection()        # round-trip input, exposed as method on the renderer
    grid.update_cell_value(...)         # command, exposed as method on the renderer
```

We want the same ergonomics for `reactive_output` and any enhanced renderers downstream packages add (`render_plotly`, `render_echart`, `render_ag_grid`, …).

## Proposed shape

```python
@render_plotly
def my_plot():
    return px.scatter(df, x=\"x\", y=\"y\")

@reactive.effect
def _():
    pts: SelectedPoints | None = my_plot.selected_points()   # round-trip input
    extent: PlotExtent | None  = my_plot.zoom_extent()       # round-trip input

@reactive.effect
@reactive.event(input.reset)
def _():
    my_plot.reset_zoom()                                     # command → custom_message
    my_plot.set_limits(x=(0, 10), y=(0, 5))                  # command → custom_message
```

Mechanics:

- **Round-trip inputs** are reactive values registered under derived names (e.g. `f\"{id}__selected_points\"`). They're exposed as callables on the renderer so the call site looks like a normal Shiny input read but doesn't need a separate `inputs.<name>` declaration.
- **Commands** are methods on the renderer that wrap `session.send_custom_message` (or the shinyreact `send_message` equivalent) and target the renderer's own ID. The user never names the message type.
- **Discovery** — round-trip inputs and commands are declared on the renderer subclass once (by the package author). Users don't re-declare them per app.

## Why this is the right home

- The renderer already captures `id` + `session` at decoration time.
- Naming collisions are bounded by the output ID — no global input-name design needed.
- Downstream packages (`shinyplotly`, `shinyshadcn`, etc.) get a clear extension point: subclass the renderer, declare round-trip inputs and commands once.
- Pairs naturally with #30 (typed Inputs/Outputs codegen): the renderer's declared round-trips become typed attributes automatically.

## Sketch of the base class API

```python
class EnhancedRenderer(Renderer[T]):
    # Declarative — package authors fill these in
    round_trip_inputs: dict[str, type] = {}     # name → type
    commands: dict[str, type] = {}              # name → payload type

    def __getattr__(self, name):
        # round_trip_inputs[name] → reactive read
        # commands[name]          → bound method that calls send_message
        ...
```

Or, more explicitly, code-generate the subclass from a declaration so attribute access is statically typed (ties into #30).

## Open questions

- **Naming**: are the JS-side input names a fixed convention (`{id}__selected_points`) or configurable per renderer? Fixed is simpler and lets the React component look them up by the parent's ID; configurable adds flexibility nobody may need.
- **Lifecycle**: how do round-trip inputs behave when the component unmounts / the output is hidden? Likely \"last value sticks until next render\" — same as Shiny inputs today.
- **Error surface for commands**: command sent before the component mounts — silently queue, or warn? Shiny's existing `update_*` family silently no-ops; matching that is probably right.
- **Async commands** (where the JS side acks): out of scope for v1; renderer methods are fire-and-forget like today's `update_*`.
- **Typing story**: exposing `selected_points: Callable[[], SelectedPoints | None]` requires either codegen (#30) or a `Generic[Inputs, Commands]` base class with `__class_getitem__` magic. Codegen is the more honest answer.
- **Discoverability**: do we want a registry so devtools can list \"every output and its round-trip inputs / commands\" for debugging?
- **Does this subsume `send_message`?** Once commands live on the renderer, the bare `send_message(session, type, data)` API is for cases without a corresponding output — worth keeping but de-emphasized.

## Out of scope

- R package equivalent.
- Two-way binding semantics (where the component owns canonical state and Python is the secondary). Renderers stay output-driven; round-trip inputs are observations of component state, not authoritative state.

title: Strongly typed Inputs/Outputs from TS source of truth
description:
## Summary

In the SPA-first model, the client decides which inputs exist (`useShinyInput<T>(\"name\", default)`) and what shape they have. Today the Python `server(inputs, output, session)` sees those inputs as `Any` — users can't get IDE completion or type checking for `inputs.move_item`, even though the JSX side already has the type.

We should generate strongly-typed `Inputs` / `Outputs` classes from the TS source so:

```python
def server(inputs: AppInputs, output, session):
    move_item: Value[MoveItemInfo] = inputs.move_item   # typed, not Any
```

## Why

- JSX is the single source of truth for input names + shapes.
- A Python-authored `TypedDict` would drift the moment someone renames an input in JSX.
- We already pay a build step in shadcn-style examples (15, 16) — adding type-gen there is cheap.
- For build-free examples (13, 14) we need a different (weaker) story.

## Proposed approach

**Primary path — codegen from TS for build-step apps:**

A `shinyreact typegen` CLI (or a Vite plugin) that:

1. Walks the project's TS/JSX with the TS Compiler API.
2. Finds every `useShinyInput<T>(name, ...)` and `useShinyOutput<T>(name)` call.
3. Extracts `name` (string literal) and `T` (TS type).
4. Emits a Python file (e.g. `app_inputs.py`) next to `app.py` containing:

```python
from shiny.reactive import Value
from typing import Protocol
from .types import MoveItemInfo  # also generated, from the TS type

class AppInputs(Protocol):
    move_item: Value[MoveItemInfo]
    # ...

class AppOutputs(Protocol):
    column_data: Value[dict[str, list[str]]]
```

- Generated values are `Value[T]` so they match Shiny's reactive access pattern.
- The TS types themselves are converted to Python (TypedDict / Pydantic / dataclass) — likely via `ts-json-schema-generator` → JSON Schema → Python, or a direct walker.
- Generated files are committed (same policy as `js/dist/`).

**Fallback path — Claude skill for build-free apps (13, 14):**

For examples that have no JS build step (the JS is inline or a single static file), provide a skill that reads the JS, infers the input/output shapes, and writes `app_inputs.py` once. No enforcement; drifts on hand edits. Documented as a convenience, not a guarantee.

## API shape

```python
from .app_inputs import AppInputs, AppOutputs

def server(inputs: AppInputs, output: AppOutputs, session):
    @reactive.effect
    @reactive.event(inputs.move_item, ignore_init=True)
    def _():
        msg: MoveItemInfo = inputs.move_item()  # callable, returns the typed value
```

`inputs.move_item` is `Value[MoveItemInfo]` (callable to read, mirrors Shiny's existing `input.foo()` access).

## Open questions

- **Dynamic input names** (e.g. `useShinyInput(\`row_\${id}\`)`): likely an escape-hatch `inputs.dynamic[\"row_42\"]: Value[T]` indexer.
- **Runtime validation**: should the generator also emit a runtime schema (Pydantic / msgspec) so a JS↔Python mismatch fails loudly with a helpful error, not just type-check noise?
- **Where the generator lives**: separate package (`shinyreact-typegen`), part of `shinyreact` Python package as a CLI entry point, or a Vite plugin in `js/`?
- **TS → Python type mapping coverage**: unions, discriminated unions, generics, `Date`. Probably restrict to JSON-serializable subset and reject the rest with a clear error.
- **No-TS users**: apps that write plain JS (ex 13, 14) get no static info. Is the skill-based fallback acceptable or do we want a runtime-declared alternative?
- **Outputs symmetry**: `useShinyOutput<T>(name)` on the JS side ↔ `@reactive_output` return type on the Python side. Generator should cross-check both directions.

## Out of scope (for now)

- R package equivalent.
- Reactive value *writes* from the JS side beyond what `useShinyInput` already covers.

title: Drop `@json-render/react` dependency — replace with in-house Spec renderer
description:
## Summary

Replace `@json-render/core` + `@json-render/react` (Vercel Labs, pre-1.0) with an in-house ~30-LOC recursive Spec renderer. The dep ships ~3,500 LOC and ~50 public exports; we use 4. Every feature beyond the `Renderer` component duplicates a model Shiny already owns.

Full proposal with rationale, trade-offs, and a future-direction section on the client-side state model: [`docs/superpowers/specs/2026-05-05-drop-json-render-dep.md`](../blob/main/docs/superpowers/specs/2026-05-05-drop-json-render-dep.md).

## What we use today

| Import | Source | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| `Renderer` | `@json-render/react` | Walks the Spec, calls registered components |
| `JSONUIProvider` | `@json-render/react` | Combines state / action / validation / visibility contexts (none of which we wire up) |
| `ComponentRegistry` (type) | `@json-render/react` | Type alias for `Record<string, ComponentType<...>>` |
| `Spec` (type) | `@json-render/core` | Flat `{ root, elements }` map |

## What we ship but don't use

State model (`StateProvider`, `useBoundProp`, `$bindState`/`$bindItem`), actions (`ActionProvider`, `ConfirmDialog`), repeat / visibility / `$computed`, AI streaming (`useUIStream`, `useChatUI`), catalog tooling (`defineRegistry`, `createRenderer`). Each duplicates Shiny's own model — Shiny owns reactive state, event dispatch, the wire transport, and (server-side) validation.

`@json-render/react` markets itself as a *generative UI framework* for AI-streamed interfaces. Right framing, wrong substrate for `shinyjson`: Shiny is the generative source, the wire is the websocket, reactive state belongs on the server.

## What we keep

- The component registry and `window.shinyjson.registerComponents(catalog, registry)` entry point — already in `js/src/registry.ts`, no dep change needed.
- The `Spec` / `Element` shape — owned in `pkg-py/src/shinyjsonold/_spec.py`. Mirror as a TypeScript type in `js/src/spec.ts`.
- The `{ element, children }` arg shape passed to registered components — preserves source compatibility for `examples/9-blended`, `examples/15-columns-shadcn`, `examples/16-shadcn`, and downstream packages.

## What replaces the renderer

```ts
function renderNode(id: string, spec: Spec, registry: Registry): ReactNode {
  const el = spec.elements[id];
  if (!el) return null;
  const Comp = registry[el.type] ?? el.type;
  const children = (el.children ?? []).map((cid) =>
    typeof cid === "string" ? renderNode(cid, spec, registry) : cid,
  );
  return typeof Comp === "string"
    ? React.createElement(Comp, el.props, ...children)
    : React.createElement(Comp, { element: el, children, key: id });
}
```

`JSONUIProvider` is removed entirely.

## Trade-offs we're accepting

- **`ValidationProvider` / `useFieldValidation`** is the one feature in the bundle that isn't redundant with Shiny. Mitigation: most downstream form packages will want their own validation primitives (zod, react-hook-form) anyway; if we later need it, ~150 LOC can be vendored from json-render's Apache-2.0 source.
- **Client-side state model** (`$bindState`, declarative path-based binding) is *not* preserved. This is a deliberate non-goal for now — see the "Future direction" section in the spec doc. Re-adoption is cheap if a concrete use case surfaces.

## Verification scope

- `examples/9-blended` (hybrid)
- `examples/15-columns-shadcn`, `examples/16-shadcn` (downstream-package pattern)
- `pkg-py/tests/old/` snapshot tests
- Any other example using `shinyjsonold`

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `@json-render/core` and `@json-render/react` removed from `js/package.json` and `js/package-lock.json`
- [ ] `js/src/renderer.tsx` and `js/src/registry.ts` no longer import from `@json-render/*`
- [ ] `js/src/spec.ts` defines `Spec`, `Element`, `ComponentRegistry` locally
- [ ] All examples render identically (visual check + existing snapshot tests)
- [ ] `pkg-py/tests/old/` passes unchanged or with reviewed snapshot diffs
- [ ] Bundle size delta reported in the PR description

## Out of scope

- JSON Patch wire format (#36)
- Renaming `shinyjson` → `shinyreact` (#38)
- Retiring `shinyjsonold` (#37) — this proposal is independent; dropping the dep is valuable whether or not `shinyjsonold` retires

## Related

- DESIGN.md §326–351 — "Why the assumption breaks down" already sketches this argument
- #37 retire `shinyjsonold`
- #38 rename to `shinyreact`
- #44 SPA vs traditional docs
